P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes. Malaysia's Foreign Exchange Policy (BNM) is liberal for current transactions. The export-proceeds conversion rule was removed, so resident exporters manage conversion to suit their cash flow. Goods export proceeds must still be repatriated within six months, extendable in exceptional circumstances. Resident individuals may freely invest foreign-currency funds sourced from abroad (other than goods export proceeds).

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Individuals, resident or non-resident, are free to open foreign-currency accounts (FCAs); banks classify individuals' FCAs as Investment FCAs under BNM's Foreign Exchange Policy Notices (Hong Leong Bank FEP fact sheet). Limits apply to converting ringgit into foreign currency for investment (see notes).

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A sole proprietorship is registered with SSM (Companies Commission of Malaysia), online via EzBiz or at a counter. The fee is RM30 a year using your personal name, or RM60 a year with a trade name (which needs Registrar approval). Registration runs 1–5 years per application. Sole proprietorships are generally for Malaysian citizens/PRs.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Malaysia taxes income derived from Malaysia. Work done while physically in Malaysia counts as Malaysian-source even if the client or employer is abroad and pay goes to a foreign account. So a freelancer working from Malaysia for foreign clients is taxable at resident rates (0% to 30%). Foreign-sourced income received by resident individuals is exempt (from 2022, originally to 31 Dec 2026, reportedly extended to 2036), except income via a Malaysian partnership.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: No VAT/GST. Malaysia levies Sales and Service Tax (SST): service tax is generally 8% on taxable services (6% for some sectors such as F&B, telecoms, construction, healthcare, education), and sales tax on goods is 5% or 10%. A service provider registers once annual taxable turnover exceeds RM500,000 for its category. The scope expanded from 1 July 2025. Whether a given freelance service is a 'taxable service' depends on the prescribed list.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The Personal Data Protection Act 2010, as amended in 2024, applies in phases. From 1 April 2025, 'data user' became 'data controller', processors gained direct security duties, and the cross-border transfer whitelist was removed. From 1 June 2025, data controllers and processors must appoint a data protection officer and notify the Commissioner of breaches, plus data subjects where significant harm is likely; data portability also applies.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw in local currency'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
